tier_reason: The yzia2000/qr_cpp_compiler README results table times GCC 13.3.0, Clang 18.1.8 and IntelLLVM 2025.3.3 on identical source; the benchmark code is public (src/implied_vol.cpp, src/svi_fit.cpp, src/greeks.cpp, python/bench.py, CMakeLists.txt with per-compiler flags, CMakePresets.json Release presets) and the CPU is named as an Emerald Rapids 5th-gen Xeon Scalable (family 6 model 207) KVM guest. Tier A holds on the precedent that a VM CPU model string without a retail SKU still counts, with that weakness kept in caveats.

corrections.claimed_speedup: icpx-fast finishes the pipeline 1.79x faster than gcc-strict (13700 ms vs 24536 ms total, single-threaded, median of 7 reps). The README text says 1.44x faster than the best non-Intel variant (clang-fast-zmm, 20453 ms), but its own table gives 1.49x (derived from page data); against gcc-fast (21554 ms) it is 1.57x (derived from page data). Under strict IEEE the field compresses to 1.00-1.23x (icpx-strict 19920 ms vs gcc-strict 24536 ms vs clang-strict 22475 ms). Stage detail for icpx-fast vs gcc-strict: SVI fit 2385 ms vs 8879 ms (3.7x) and greeks 770 ms vs 2571 ms (3.3x); on the Newton IV stage gcc-fast is faster (3.07 vs 2.83 Mq/s).
corrections.license: Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception (intel/llvm LICENSE.TXT, the open-source base); the benchmarked icpx 2025.3.3 binary and its SVML/libimf runtimes came from the proprietary intel/oneapi-basekit image
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is a small personal repo (0 stars, 0 forks, no LICENSE file, 8 commits on 2026-08-01/02, all co-authored by 'claude', i.e. AI-assisted) on a transcendental-heavy workload chosen to favour SVML; one session on a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM, so numbers are relative; CPU SKU is masked (only family 6 model 207, Emerald Rapids), so tier A is borderline. The README's headline '1.44x faster than the best non-Intel variant' is an arithmetic slip; its own table gives 1.49x. Most of the gain comes from Intel's proprietary math runtimes (SVML vector erf/exp/log in the SVI and greeks sweeps, and libimf's faster scalar erf/exp in the IV loop per the README appendix), which are not part of the open-source intel/llvm repo that repo_url points at. The README and src/implied_vol.cpp say glibc's libmvec has no vector erf, but current glibc's sysdeps/x86/fpu/bits/math-vector.h declares __DECL_SIMD_erf for x86_64 under __FAST_MATH__, so the stated reason the gcc/clang fast-math builds stay scalar is doubtful and those baselines may be under-tuned (clang's -fveclib=libmvec mapping may also lack erf). Only gcc gets -funroll-loops. Cross-compiler validation (results/validation.md: all nine builds agree to about 2e-14 vol points) was run on quotes_dev.pcap (298,720 quotes), not the 29.9M-quote timed file. The README notes gcc-fast beats icpx-fast on the Newton IV stage (3.07 vs 2.83 Mq/s), strict-IEEE advantage is only 1.23x, and forcing 512-bit vectors made icpx 14.8% slower. Corroboration, opened: LAMMPS issue #5213 (akohlmey, 2026-09-25, 2x20-core Xeon Gold 6248 Cascade Lake, RHEL 10; icpx 2026.1 -xHost -fp-model fast=2 relative to GCC 14 '-sf intel') reports icpx at lj 1.70, rhodo 1.62, eam 1.17, sw 1.85, water 1.88, airebo 1.85, tersoff 1.49, snap 3.48, but lc 0.91 and dpd 1.02, so it is not uniformly faster. Counter-evidence, opened by the search agent: gist kaityo256/d41481467df504c5039715d38954ab8a shows GCC 40-60x faster than ICC 18-19.1 on a degenerate std::uniform_real_distribution loop. Search-snippet only: SPEC withdrew over 2,000 SPEC CPU 2017 results that used a benchmark-specific oneAPI DPC++ optimization. The listed 'Intel C++ Compiler' is the proprietary product; intel/llvm's README says it is a technical foundation for the oneAPI DPC++ Compiler and that feature parity with downstream products is not guaranteed.

notes: Every table number in the record matches the README; only the '1.44x vs best non-Intel' headline is wrong on the page itself (table gives 1.49x), now corrected. Metadata checked: intel/llvm 1.5k stars, 863 forks, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-10-06 on the sycl branch; license refined to Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception. Shortcomings to record: AI-assisted 0-star single-session cloud-VM benchmark with masked SKU, proprietary SVML/libimf carry the win, gcc/clang fast-math baselines possibly under-tuned (libmvec does declare vector erf), validation on a smaller dev file.

tier_reason: nodejs/node issue #55208 gives only an approximate '~2.5 slower' for ClangCL with no hardware, versions, flags or timings, and the issue itself attributes the gap to ClangCL builds not using precompiled headers while MSVC builds did; PR #55249 enabled PCH for clang-cl and 'improves ClangCL compilation time drastically'. The only number therefore measures PCH versus no PCH (a crippled baseline, AssemblyScript precedent), not compiler speed at equal settings, leaving only directional evidence.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Issue #55208 (StefanStojanovic, 2024-10-01): 'ClangCL compilation is ~2.5 slower (less with x64, more with ARM64)' than MSVC when building Node.js with vcbuild.bat, attributed to ClangCL not using precompiled headers while MSVC did. PR #55249 (merged 2024-10-11) enabled PCH for clang-cl and states it 'improves ClangCL compilation time drastically'; no before/after or MSVC-vs-ClangCL numbers are given, so no valid equal-settings ratio exists on the page.
corrections.caveats: Single issue report by a Node.js Windows build contributor with no hardware, compiler versions, flags or raw timings; the stated cause is that MSVC used precompiled headers and clang-cl did not, and the issue was closed by Node.js PR #55249 which enables PCH for clang-cl, so the 2.5x gap measured a build-configuration difference and is obsolete. MSVC is a closed binary with no repo; usability reference. Counter-evidence on generated-code speed, opened: simdjson issue #847 (jkeiser, 2020-05-01) 'MSVC simdjson twice as slow as ClangCL': twitter.json overall 1.3051 (MSVC 19.25.28614) vs 2.2221 (ClangCL 9.0.0), stage 1 2.3777 vs 5.4161, stage 2 3.3898 vs 4.6401; issue #812 shows the same pattern (per the search agent). Weak extra compile-time data (search agent): vcpkg issue #15961, about 36 s MSVC on Windows vs about 1 min 10 s GCC under WSL, different platforms, no versions or flags. Search-snippet only (pages blocked, not opened): Daniel Lemire's 2023-02-27 post 'Visual Studio versus ClangCL' (VS 2022, ClangCL on LLVM 15, i7-11370 Tiger Lake, simdutf) says compiling with ClangCL takes much longer and that in Debug MSVC compiles faster, while ClangCL Release code can be up to 40% faster; a llama.cpp PR #10668 snippet attributes a 3-4x clang build slowdown to MSVC spawning parallel cl processes (/MP), another configuration artifact; a Chrome team post reportedly says building Chrome with Clang is about 15% slower than MSVC. The docs.microsoft.com URL in the list is a C++/CLI page with no performance data; learn.microsoft.com and Microsoft devblogs were blocked.

notes: Issue and PR opened: the ~2.5x figure is real but it measures MSVC-with-PCH vs clang-cl-without-PCH and was fixed by PR #55249, so downgrade C to D (crippled-baseline precedent, not a reject). Shortcomings to record: no methodology, configuration artifact rather than compiler speed, gap closed in Oct 2024, and MSVC-generated code is slower than ClangCL (simdjson #847, 1.3051 vs 2.2221 GB/s, ClangCL 1.70x faster, derived from page data). Lemire's 2023 post (snippet only) is the best lead for an equal-settings compile-time comparison if lemire.me becomes reachable.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: besides the first-party lld docs table (stated hardware, no programs, command lines or harness, so C on its own), the independent Wild linker project's benchmark page (benchmarks/ryzen-9955hx.md, AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX 16-core, 92 GiB RAM, output on tmpfs, 99% confidence intervals) times GNU ld 2.46 and LLD 21.1.8 (Ubuntu packages) on the same inputs and shows lld 1.06x to 12x faster. Not A because the captured link inputs and the build flags of the linked programs are not published there.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent (Wild benchmark page, AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX, GNU ld 2.46 vs LLD 21.1.8, chart labels relative to Wild 0.10.0): lld links ripgrep 4.9x, wild-debug 7.0x, mold-gdb-index 12.1x and rust-hello-world 2.0x faster than GNU ld, with near parity on c-hello-world (1.06x) and linker-plugin LTO wild-lto (1.12x) (all derived from page data). First-party lld docs table (lld/docs/index.md, about 2017, 2-socket 20-core Xeon E5-2680 2.80 GHz with SSD), lld w/threads vs GNU gold w/threads: ffmpeg dbg 0.35s vs 1.01s, mysqld dbg 0.68s vs 2.68s, clang dbg 5.28s vs 23.49s, chromium dbg 16.70s vs 60.82s; GNU ld took 1.72s, 8.50s, 104.03s and 209.05s on the same four programs. Docs text: 'you can expect that LLD runs more than twice as fast as the GNU gold linker' on a large program on a multicore machine.
corrections.hardware: Independent run: AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX 16-core/32-thread, 92 GiB RAM, output on tmpfs. lld docs table: 2-socket 20-core 40-thread Xeon E5-2680 2.80 GHz with an SSD drive
corrections.caveats: The lld docs table is first-party, undated but from about 2017 (the same page says 'as of February 2017'; the file was rewritten to Markdown on 2026-07-16 without changing the table); the four programs, link command lines, compiler and flags are not given. GNU ld rows drop -icf=all and -gdb-index because GNU ld lacks them (footnote says GNU ld would be slower with them). The docs warn results vary with cores, memory and disk. The independent Wild benchmark covers GNU ld (BFD) only in a few charts and has no GNU gold rows; its captured inputs are not published, the ratios are derived from chart percentage labels relative to Wild 0.10.0, and the mold-gdb-index case may favour lld if GNU ld lacks --gdb-index. Gains shrink to near parity on tiny programs (c-hello-world 1.06x) and with linker-plugin LTO (wild-lto 1.12x). Newer linkers are much faster than lld: on the same Wild page lld is +519% vs Wild 0.10.0 on chrome and +207% on clang-debug, and mold's README (August 2026, Threadripper 7980X, inputs on Zenodo) reports mold 4.9x faster than lld at the median (mold's author is lld's original developer). llvm-project is already in the catalog (AddressSanitizer entry), hence the paper:llvm-lld-linker id. The 'LLVM' list entry is a collection; lld is the component with the clearest numeric comparison found. A numeric Clang-vs-GCC compile-time comparison was not found on a reachable page (blog.llvm.org blocked).

notes: lld docs numbers match the record exactly; I upgraded C to B on Wild's independent GNU ld 2.46 vs LLD 21.1.8 benchmark and moved benchmark_url there, keeping the docs table in claimed_speedup (the docs URL is https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/lld/docs/index.md). Metadata checked: llvm-project about 41k stars, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception (LICENSE.TXT), not archived; last_commit 2026-10-06 not re-checked but plausible. Shortcomings to record: docs table is 2017-era first-party without command lines, independent page lacks gold and published inputs, near parity on small or LTO links, mold and wild are several times faster than lld.
